packs.title: Everyday Kanji: Levels 1–5
packs.description: High-utility everyday vocabulary whose newest WaniKani kanji falls between levels 1 and 5.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Exactly <kanji>one</kanji> portion enters your <kanji>mouth</kanji>: <vocabulary>one bite</vocabulary>, or a <vocabulary>mouthful</vocabulary>.

一口 can count a single bite of food or a single sip of a drink, as in 一口食べる and 一口飲む.
words.readingMnemonic: One 一 carries its familiar ひと sound toward a gigantic mouth 口 carrying くち: <reading>ひと—くち</reading>. It drops in exactly one strawberry, and the jaws snap shut after that single <vocabulary>mouthful</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>one bite</vocabulary>. 一口 can also be one sip when the thing consumed is a drink.

contextSentences.ja: ケーキを一口食べた。
contextSentences.en: I ate one bite of cake.

contextSentences.ja: 一口飲めば、味が分かります。
contextSentences.en: One sip will tell you how it tastes.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Picture the craftsperson entrusted with <kanji>big</kanji> <kanji>construction</kanji>: the <vocabulary>carpenter</vocabulary> shaping the building's wood by hand.

大工 usually means a carpenter who builds or repairs wooden structures, rather than a construction worker in general.
words.readingMnemonic: A cuckoo clock collapses on its builder, and the bird shrieks <reading>DIE—COO!</reading> The <vocabulary>carpenter</vocabulary> ducks, then rebuilds the wooden clock even bigger. 大工 specifically means a carpenter, not every kind of construction worker.

contextSentences.ja: 父は大工として働いている。
contextSentences.en: My father works as a carpenter.

contextSentences.ja: 大工が古い家を直した。
contextSentences.en: A carpenter repaired the old house.

words.meaningMnemonic:
When something <kanji>enter</kanji>s your <kanji>hand</kanji>, you <vocabulary>obtain</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>acquire</vocabulary> it.

入手 is a noun or する verb used for getting an item or information, especially something sought out or not immediately available.
words.readingMnemonic: A sneaker collector tears open a locked crate and gasps, <reading>NEW SHOE!</reading> Getting that rare shoe into her hands means she can finally <vocabulary>obtain</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>acquire</vocabulary> it. 入手する is common for acquiring an item or information.

contextSentences.ja: 限定の切符を入手した。
contextSentences.en: I obtained a limited-edition ticket.

contextSentences.ja: 必要な情報はネットで入手できます。
contextSentences.en: You can obtain the necessary information online.

words.meaningMnemonic:
The <kanji>evening</kanji> <kanji>sun</kanji> glowing low on the horizon is the <vocabulary>evening sun</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>setting sun</vocabulary>.

夕日 refers to the sun itself near sunset; 夕焼け instead describes the red evening sky or sunset glow.
words.readingMnemonic: A photographer points at two friends and cries <reading>YOU—HE!</reading> They race up a hill before the <vocabulary>setting sun</vocabulary> slips below the sea. 夕日 is the evening sun itself, especially when seen near sunset.

contextSentences.ja: 海に沈む夕日がきれいだ。
contextSentences.en: The setting sun over the sea is beautiful.

contextSentences.ja: 夕日を見ながら家に帰った。
contextSentences.en: I went home while watching the evening sun.

words.meaningMnemonic:
The <kanji>main</kanji> <kanji>day</kanji> under discussion is <vocabulary>today</vocabulary>—in effect, <vocabulary>this day</vocabulary>.

本日 is more formal than 今日 and is common in announcements, business speech, schedules, and customer-facing notices.
words.readingMnemonic: A book 本 carrying ほん lands on a calendar day 日 carrying じつ: <reading>ほん—じつ</reading>. The calendar seals shut at midnight, so the event must happen <vocabulary>today</vocabulary>. 本日 is a formal or businesslike way to refer to today.

contextSentences.ja: 本日は休業いたします。
contextSentences.en: We are closed today.

contextSentences.ja: 本日の会議は三時からです。
contextSentences.en: Today's meeting starts at three.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Repeat one <kanji>day</kanji> with the 々 mark and the days march on <vocabulary>day by day</vocabulary>, forming your <vocabulary>daily</vocabulary> life.

日々 can be a noun, an adverb, or modify another noun with の, and it often emphasizes ongoing change or repeated everyday effort.
words.readingMnemonic: Every calendar page develops a new ひび, a crack, as another day passes. Those exact-homophone <reading>ひび</reading> spread <vocabulary>day by day</vocabulary> until the whole <vocabulary>daily</vocabulary> calendar is cracked. 日々 describes repeated days or something happening continually over them.

contextSentences.ja: 日々の練習が力になる。
contextSentences.en: Daily practice makes you stronger.

contextSentences.ja: 町は日々変わっている。
contextSentences.en: The town is changing day by day.

words.meaningMnemonic:
The <kanji>real</kanji> <kanji>person</kanji>—not a representative or a rumor—is <vocabulary>the person themself</vocabulary>, the <vocabulary>person in question</vocabulary>.

本人 identifies the actual individual concerned and is useful when confirming something directly with them or contrasting them with someone acting on their behalf.
words.readingMnemonic: A book 本 marked ほん opens, and a person 人 marked にん climbs out: <reading>ほん—にん</reading>. The masked stand-in is ejected because the clerk needs <vocabulary>the person themself</vocabulary>, the <vocabulary>person in question</vocabulary>. 本人 contrasts the actual person with a representative or what others report.

contextSentences.ja: 本人に直接確認してください。
contextSentences.en: Please confirm it directly with the person themself.

contextSentences.ja: その話は本人から聞きました。
contextSentences.en: I heard that story from the person in question.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Your <kanji>hand</kanji> follows the pattern in a <kanji>book</kanji>, using it as a <vocabulary>model</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>example</vocabulary> to copy.

手本 is a concrete demonstration or an exemplary person or work; 手本にする means to use something or someone as a model.
words.readingMnemonic: A hand 手 carrying て reaches into a book 本 carrying ほん and pulls out a perfect demonstration: <reading>て—ほん</reading>. Every student copies the hand exactly because it is the official <vocabulary>model</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>example</vocabulary>. 手本 is something worth imitating or a demonstration to follow.

contextSentences.ja: 先生が手本を見せた。
contextSentences.en: The teacher showed us an example.

contextSentences.ja: 姉を手本にして勉強している。
contextSentences.en: I study with my older sister as my model.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Imagine <kanji>one</kanji> sweeping <kanji>cut</kanji> taking the whole pile at once: it takes <vocabulary>everything</vocabulary>, entirely.

一切 means the whole of something, but with a negative predicate it becomes emphatic <vocabulary>not at all</vocabulary>, as in 一切かかりません.
words.readingMnemonic: A magician slices the H off HISS, leaving <reading>ISS—SIGH</reading>, then sighs as every prop disappears. The two s sounds meet in the cut, and <vocabulary>everything</vocabulary> vanishes; with a negative command, not one prop returns. 一切 often means “not at all” when paired with a negative verb.

contextSentences.ja: 費用は一切かかりません。
contextSentences.en: It will not cost anything at all.

contextSentences.ja: 一切の責任は私が負います。
contextSentences.en: I will take full responsibility.

words.meaningMnemonic:
The <kanji>middle</kanji> of the <kanji>heart</kanji> is the <vocabulary>center</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>core</vocabulary> around which everything else gathers.

中心 works for physical centers and abstract focal points; Xを中心に means centered on or mainly around X.
words.readingMnemonic: A dog finds an enormous shin bone and <reading>CHEW—SHIN</reading> marks the exact spot it gnaws. It drills straight into the <vocabulary>center</vocabulary> until only the <vocabulary>core</vocabulary> remains. 中心 can be a physical center or the central focus of an activity.

contextSentences.ja: 駅を中心に店が増えた。
contextSentences.en: More shops have opened around the station.

contextSentences.ja: 町の中心に公園がある。
contextSentences.en: There is a park in the center of town.

words.meaningMnemonic:
An <kanji>old</kanji> <kanji>book</kanji> that has already had an owner is a <vocabulary>used book</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>secondhand book</vocabulary>.

古本 refers specifically to previously owned books and appears in compounds such as 古本屋, a used-book shop.
words.readingMnemonic: An old book opens and unfolds into a <reading>FULL HORN</reading> that blasts dust across the shop. Only a battered <vocabulary>used book</vocabulary> could hide an instrument that worn. 古本 means a secondhand book, whether or not it looks visibly old.

contextSentences.ja: 古本を三冊買った。
contextSentences.en: I bought three used books.

contextSentences.ja: この古本には前の持ち主のメモがある。
contextSentences.en: This secondhand book has notes from its previous owner.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Before committing, go <kanji>below</kanji> the surface and <kanji>see</kanji> the place for yourself; that early visit is a <vocabulary>preview</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>advance inspection</vocabulary>.

下見 is commonly used for checking a room, venue, route, or location ahead of the real event, often with 下見する or 下見に行く.
words.readingMnemonic: Before surgery, she examines a giant model stomach while chanting <reading>SHE—TUMMY</reading>. That careful look beforehand is a <vocabulary>preview</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>advance inspection</vocabulary>. 下見 is commonly used for checking a home, venue, or location before deciding.

contextSentences.ja: 引っ越す前に部屋を下見した。
contextSentences.en: I inspected the room before moving.

contextSentences.ja: 明日は会場の下見に行きます。
contextSentences.en: Tomorrow I am going to preview the venue.

words.meaningMnemonic:
<kanji>One</kanji> compact thing you <kanji>say</kanji> is <vocabulary>a word</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>brief comment</vocabulary>.

一言 usually means a short remark rather than one dictionary word; 一言お願いします invites someone to say a few words.
words.readingMnemonic: The number one 一 carries its ひと sound to a word 言 carrying こと: <reading>ひと—こと</reading>. The conductor permits one <vocabulary>brief comment</vocabulary>, then drops the curtain before a second can escape. 一言 often means a brief remark rather than literally one lexical word.

contextSentences.ja: 最後に一言お願いします。
contextSentences.en: Please say a few words at the end.

contextSentences.ja: 彼の一言で安心した。
contextSentences.en: A single comment from him reassured me.

words.meaningMnemonic:
One <kanji>generation</kanji> gives way to the next <kanji>era</kanji>; each group shaped by its time is a <vocabulary>generation</vocabulary>.

世代 groups people by age or historical period and often appears in expressions such as 若い世代 and 世代によって.
words.readingMnemonic: The world 世 carries せ on a relay baton and hands it to an era 代 carrying だい: <reading>せ—だい</reading>. Each handoff replaces grandparents with children and reveals the next <vocabulary>generation</vocabulary>. 世代 groups people by the era or stage of life they share.

contextSentences.ja: 若い世代にも人気がある。
contextSentences.en: It is also popular with the younger generation.

contextSentences.ja: 世代によって考え方が違う。
contextSentences.en: Ways of thinking differ by generation.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Take <kanji>what</kanji> and add the uncertain か: the unknown answer becomes <vocabulary>something</vocabulary>, or in a question, <vocabulary>anything</vocabulary>.

何か is an indefinite pronoun. In 何か飲みますか it means something, while an English translation may naturally use anything.
words.readingMnemonic: What 何 carries なに into a mystery box, and the question marker か springs out behind it: <reading>なに—か?</reading> The spring launches <vocabulary>something</vocabulary> unknown into the air, but nobody can tell what. 何か usually refers to an unspecified something; in questions, English may render it as ‘anything.’

contextSentences.ja: 何か飲みますか。
contextSentences.en: Would you like something to drink?

contextSentences.ja: 机の下に何か落ちている。
contextSentences.en: Something has fallen under the desk.

packs.title: Everyday Kanji: Levels 6–10
packs.description: High-utility everyday vocabulary whose newest WaniKani kanji falls between levels 6 and 10.

words.meaningMnemonic:
You <kanji>take</kanji> hold of a door with your <kanji>hand</kanji> by grabbing its <vocabulary>handle</vocabulary>.

取っ手 is the part you grip on a door, drawer, pot, or container; depending on its shape, English may call it a handle, grip, or knob.
words.readingMnemonic: The 取 hand reaches for 手, but the handle catches the two t sounds together: <reading>TO—TTE!</reading> It will not let go until you grab the <vocabulary>handle</vocabulary> yourself. 取っ手 is the part you grip on a door, drawer, pot, or container.

contextSentences.ja: ドアの取っ手を回した。
contextSentences.en: I turned the door handle.

contextSentences.ja: 鍋の取っ手が熱くなっている。
contextSentences.en: The handle of the pot is hot.

words.meaningMnemonic:
The <kanji>main</kanji> thing you <kanji>eat</kanji> at meal after meal is your <vocabulary>staple food</vocabulary>.

主食 means the central carbohydrate or food a diet is built around, such as rice, bread, or noodles, not simply a favorite dish.
words.readingMnemonic: A chef lifts the rice lid and finds a boot inside: <reading>SHOE—SHOCK!</reading> The shoe has replaced rice as the meal's <vocabulary>staple food</vocabulary>, shocking every diner. 主食 is the main starch or food regularly supporting meals.

contextSentences.ja: 日本では米が主食だ。
contextSentences.en: Rice is a staple food in Japan.

contextSentences.ja: 私の主食はパンです。
contextSentences.en: Bread is my staple food.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Stand on a calendar square marked <kanji>now</kanji> and point down the row to every date <kanji>later</kanji>: that future is <vocabulary>from now on</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>hereafter</vocabulary>.

今後 points to the future from the present and is common in plans, forecasts, and the polite expression 今後もよろしくお願いします.
words.readingMnemonic: A time traveler lands in <reading>CONGO</reading> and plants a sign that points only forward. Everything beyond the sign happens <vocabulary>from now on</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>hereafter</vocabulary>. 今後 refers to the future from the present point, often in plans or polite promises.

contextSentences.ja: 今後の予定を確認しましょう。
contextSentences.en: Let's review our plans going forward.

contextSentences.ja: 今後もよろしくお願いします。
contextSentences.en: I look forward to continuing to work with you.

words.meaningMnemonic:
A meal makes an <kanji>exit</kanji> from the restaurant and arrives at your <kanji>front</kanji> door: <vocabulary>food delivery</vocabulary>.

出前 traditionally refers to a restaurant delivering prepared food; 出前を取る means to order delivery.
words.readingMnemonic: Food bursts out of 出 carrying で and lands in front 前 carrying まえ: <reading>で—まえ</reading>. A customer opens the door to find the restaurant's <vocabulary>food delivery</vocabulary> steaming on the mat. 出前 traditionally refers to prepared food delivered by a restaurant.

contextSentences.ja: 昼は寿司の出前を取った。
contextSentences.en: We ordered sushi delivery for lunch.

contextSentences.ja: この店は出前もしています。
contextSentences.en: This restaurant also makes deliveries.

words.meaningMnemonic:
The <kanji>inside</kanji> of the body has its own medical <kanji>department</kanji>: <vocabulary>internal medicine</vocabulary>.

内科 can mean the field, an internal-medicine department, or a clinic; it contrasts with surgery-oriented 外科.
words.readingMnemonic: The inside kanji 内 carries ない into a clinic department 科 carrying か: <reading>ない—か</reading>. Doctors inside a giant model stomach treat fevers and internal illness in the <vocabulary>internal medicine</vocabulary> department. 内科 is the hospital department or clinic for non-surgical internal conditions.

contextSentences.ja: 熱が続くので内科に行った。
contextSentences.en: I went to an internal medicine clinic because my fever wouldn't go away.

contextSentences.ja: 内科は二階にあります。
contextSentences.en: The internal medicine department is on the second floor.

words.meaningMnemonic:
A screen hangs <kanji>above</kanji> the audience and begins to <kanji>reflect</kanji> a film across its full width: a <vocabulary>screening</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>showing</vocabulary>.

上映 refers to publicly showing a film or video on a screen; 上映する is to screen it, and 上映時間 is its showing time.
words.readingMnemonic: Movie star Joe A. pedals a projector while the crowd chants <reading>JOE—A!</reading> The film appears only while he pedals, turning his workout into a public <vocabulary>screening</vocabulary>. 上映 refers to showing a film or video on a screen.

contextSentences.ja: その映画は来週上映される。
contextSentences.en: That movie will be screened next week.

contextSentences.ja: 上映の時間を確認した。
contextSentences.en: I checked the screening time.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Draw a timeline <kanji>from</kanji> a past event to every day that has <kanji>come</kanji> after it; the whole stretch is <vocabulary>since</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>ever since</vocabulary> that event.

以来 follows a time or event and continues through the present, as in 卒業以来 for ever since graduation.
words.readingMnemonic: Eli tells one enormous lie, and the town clock freezes at that instant: <reading>E—LIE</reading>. <vocabulary>Ever since</vocabulary> that lie, every later event is measured from the frozen clock. 以来 follows the event or time that serves as the starting point.

contextSentences.ja: 卒業以来、彼に会っていない。
contextSentences.en: I have not seen him since graduation.

contextSentences.ja: 先月以来、雨が少ない。
contextSentences.en: There has been little rain since last month.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Measure <kanji>from</kanji> the boundary toward the <kanji>inside</kanji> and stay <vocabulary>within</vocabulary> it, using <vocabulary>no more than</vocabulary> the stated limit.

以内 includes the endpoint: 三日以内 means within three days, including the third day.
words.readingMnemonic: A guard paints a boundary around the playground; anyone beyond it becomes <reading>いない</reading>—“not there.” To remain <vocabulary>within</vocabulary> the limit, every child must stay inside the line. 以内 includes the stated maximum, as in “within three days.”

contextSentences.ja: 三日以内に返事をください。
contextSentences.en: Please reply within three days.

contextSentences.ja: 駅から十分以内で行けます。
contextSentences.en: You can get there from the station within ten minutes.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Picture the <kanji>world</kanji> packed into the shared <kanji>interval</kanji> between private lives; there <vocabulary>society</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>the public</vocabulary> watch and talk.

世間 often means the surrounding public and its social expectations, as in 世間の目 or 世間の反応, rather than society as an institution.
words.readingMnemonic: The world 世 carries せ into the space 間 carrying けん: <reading>せ—けん</reading>. The entire public crowds into that tiny space to judge one hat, turning it into all of <vocabulary>society</vocabulary>'s business. 世間 often means the public and its shared opinions.

contextSentences.ja: 世間の反応は厳しかった。
contextSentences.en: The public reaction was harsh.

contextSentences.ja: そのニュースは世間で話題になった。
contextSentences.en: That news became a topic of public conversation.

words.meaningMnemonic:
The <kanji>middle</kanji> conceals the real <kanji>body</kanji> of the thing: its <vocabulary>contents</vocabulary>, or what is <vocabulary>inside</vocabulary>.

中身 can describe what is inside a container and, figuratively, a person's or proposal's substance rather than outward appearance.
words.readingMnemonic: The middle 中 carries なか as a plain box splits open, and a body 身 carrying み leaps out: <reading>なか—み</reading>. That tiny body is the surprising <vocabulary>contents</vocabulary> hidden <vocabulary>inside</vocabulary>. 中身 can also mean substance or character beneath outward appearance.

contextSentences.ja: 箱の中身を確認した。
contextSentences.en: I checked the contents of the box.

contextSentences.ja: 見た目より中身が大切だ。
contextSentences.en: What is inside matters more than appearance.

words.meaningMnemonic:
The <kanji>main</kanji> <kanji>duty</kanji> in the story belongs to its <vocabulary>leading role</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>main character</vocabulary>.

主役 applies to a lead performer or central figure, and it can figuratively name the person or thing receiving the spotlight.
words.readingMnemonic: A yak in sparkling shoes barges onto the stage: <reading>SHOE—YAK</reading>. It steals the spotlight and becomes the show's <vocabulary>main character</vocabulary> in the <vocabulary>leading role</vocabulary>. 主役 can also be the central person at a real event.

contextSentences.ja: 彼女が映画の主役を演じる。
contextSentences.en: She plays the leading role in the movie.

contextSentences.ja: 今日の主役は新郎と新婦です。
contextSentences.en: Today's main characters are the bride and groom.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Your <kanji>body</kanji> is what you <kanji>investigate</kanji> when checking your <vocabulary>physical condition</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>state of health</vocabulary>.

体調 describes how well or unwell someone feels overall; 体調が悪い and 体調を整える are common patterns.
words.readingMnemonic: The BODY 体 walks into CONDITION 調's clinic, and the two kanji snap their familiar sounds together: <reading>たい—ちょう</reading>. The clinic's scanner turns green only when the patient's <vocabulary>physical condition</vocabulary> is healthy. 体調 usually describes how someone is feeling physically.

contextSentences.ja: 今日は体調がよくない。
contextSentences.en: I am not feeling well today.

contextSentences.ja: 体調を整えて試合に備える。
contextSentences.en: I will get into good physical condition for the match.

packs.title: Everyday Kanji: Levels 11–15
packs.description: High-utility everyday vocabulary whose newest WaniKani kanji falls between levels 11 and 15.

words.meaningMnemonic:
<kanji>Transmit</kanji> what someone wants to <kanji>say</kanji> and it becomes a <vocabulary>message</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>verbal message</vocabulary>.

伝言 is especially a message entrusted to another person to pass along; 伝言をお願いする is a common way to leave one.
words.readingMnemonic: A spy hides a note in a den, then disappears: <reading>DEN—GONE</reading>. The next agent finds the <vocabulary>message</vocabulary> after its sender is gone. 伝言 is information passed through another person, often a verbal message.

contextSentences.ja: 田中さんに伝言をお願いできますか。
contextSentences.en: Could I leave a message for Mr. Tanaka?

contextSentences.ja: 田中さんが帰ったら、この伝言を伝えます。
contextSentences.en: I'll pass on this message when Mr. Tanaka returns.

words.meaningMnemonic:
A carrier pigeon offers the <kanji>convenience</kanji> of crossing the distance with <vocabulary>news</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>tidings</vocabulary>, or a personal <vocabulary>letter</vocabulary> tied to its leg.

便り refers to news or correspondence from someone, often when the sender is elsewhere, as in 母からの便り.
words.readingMnemonic: A carrier pigeon is the one creature you can rely on—your 頼り—and it arrives carrying a 便り. The two words share the exact sound <reading>たより</reading>, so that trusted bird brings <vocabulary>news</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>letter</vocabulary>. 便り can be correspondence or word about how someone is doing.

contextSentences.ja: 母から元気だという便りが届いた。
contextSentences.en: News arrived from my mother saying that she is well.

contextSentences.ja: 旅先から便りを送ります。
contextSentences.en: I will send a letter from my travels.

words.meaningMnemonic:
A thread pulls several objects <kanji>together</kanji>, then must <kanji>pass through</kanji> every one; the thread is what they have in <vocabulary>common</vocabulary>, a <vocabulary>shared</vocabulary> feature.

共通 can be a noun or modifier, while 共通する describes a feature shared by multiple people or things.
words.readingMnemonic: On a calendar marked 今日（きょう）, TWO actors receive one shared ticket: <reading>今日—TWO</reading>. Because both enter with the same pass, it is <vocabulary>common</vocabulary> to them and visibly <vocabulary>shared</vocabulary>. 共通 describes a feature, interest, or element held in common.

contextSentences.ja: 共通の趣味がきっかけで友達になった。
contextSentences.en: We became friends through a shared hobby.

contextSentences.ja: 二つの案には共通する点がある。
contextSentences.en: The two proposals have something in common.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Gain a <kanji>benefit</kanji> by putting something to <kanji>use</kanji>: you <vocabulary>use</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>utilize</vocabulary> it.

利用する often means making practical use of a service, facility, system, opportunity, or information.
words.readingMnemonic: Lee grabs a giant yo-yo and cries <reading>LEE—YO!</reading> She turns the toy into a crane, proving she can <vocabulary>use</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>utilize</vocabulary> anything. 利用する is used for making practical use of a service, facility, or thing.

contextSentences.ja: この券は何度でも利用できます。
contextSentences.en: You can use this pass any number of times.

contextSentences.ja: 仕事の帰りに図書館を利用する。
contextSentences.en: I use the library on my way home from work.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Give an outfit the muted <kanji>earth</kanji> <kanji>flavor</kanji> of soil and clay and it looks <vocabulary>plain</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>subdued</vocabulary>, and unflashy.

地味 describes appearance or activity that does not stand out; it can be neutral, approvingly modest, or mildly critical depending on context.
words.readingMnemonic: Jimmy arrives at a glitter party in a gray sweater and whispers <reading>JIMMY</reading>. His completely <vocabulary>plain</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>subdued</vocabulary> outfit makes him disappear against the wall. 地味 can describe appearance, work, or behavior that is unflashy.

contextSentences.ja: 彼は地味な服を好む。
contextSentences.en: He prefers plain clothes.

contextSentences.ja: 地味な作業だが、とても大切だ。
contextSentences.en: It is unglamorous work, but it is very important.

words.meaningMnemonic:
As something <kanji>become</kanji>s a whole, every <kanji>part</kanji> that forms it is a <vocabulary>component</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>ingredient</vocabulary>.

成分 is used for the constituent substances in food, medicine, cosmetics, materials, and living bodies.
words.readingMnemonic: A talking bun demands that the baker name every item inside it: <reading>SAY—BUN!</reading> Flour, yeast, and salt each leap out as an <vocabulary>ingredient</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>component</vocabulary>. 成分 is common on labels for chemical or nutritional contents.

contextSentences.ja: 買う前に食品の成分を確認した。
contextSentences.en: I checked the food's ingredients before buying it.

contextSentences.ja: 水は体の大切な成分です。
contextSentences.en: Water is an important component of the body.

words.meaningMnemonic:
As something <kanji>become</kanji>s <kanji>long</kanji>er, you can see its <vocabulary>growth</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>development</vocabulary>.

成長 applies to physical growth and to the development of people, skills, organizations, or economies; 成長する is the usual verb.
words.readingMnemonic: BECOME 成 plants itself beside LONG 長, and their familiar sounds lock together: <reading>せい—ちょう</reading>. A seedling instantly stretches past the roof, making its <vocabulary>growth</vocabulary> impossible to miss. 成長 covers physical growth and personal or organizational development.

contextSentences.ja: 子どもの成長は早い。
contextSentences.en: Children grow quickly.

contextSentences.ja: 失敗も成長につながります。
contextSentences.en: Failure also leads to growth.

words.meaningMnemonic:
<kanji>Above</kanji> all your other clothes, you <kanji>wear</kanji> a <vocabulary>jacket</vocabulary> or other <vocabulary>outerwear</vocabulary>.

上着 is a general outer layer such as a jacket or coat, especially one you can put on or take off over an outfit.
words.readingMnemonic: A puppy trots in wearing an oversized jacket, and the crowd squeals <reading>OOH—WAGGY!</reading> Its wagging tail spins the <vocabulary>jacket</vocabulary> and all its <vocabulary>outerwear</vocabulary> around like a propeller. 上着 means an outer garment worn over other clothes.

contextSentences.ja: 寒いので上着を着てください。
contextSentences.en: It is cold, so please put on a jacket.

contextSentences.ja: 上着を椅子に掛けた。
contextSentences.en: I hung my jacket on the chair.

words.meaningMnemonic:
In the <kanji>middle</kanji> of the building sits a sheltered <kanji>garden</kanji>: the <vocabulary>courtyard</vocabulary>.

中庭 is an open or garden space surrounded partly or completely by a building.
words.readingMnemonic: The middle 中 carries なか into a mansion, where a garden 庭 carrying にわ is trapped between four walls: <reading>なか—にわ</reading>. The hidden <vocabulary>courtyard</vocabulary> is enclosed by the building and cannot spill into the street. 中庭 is an inner courtyard rather than an ordinary yard.

contextSentences.ja: ホテルの中庭で朝食を食べた。
contextSentences.en: We ate breakfast in the hotel's courtyard.

contextSentences.ja: 中庭には小さな池がある。
contextSentences.en: There is a small pond in the courtyard.

words.meaningMnemonic:
People <kanji>mix</kanji> while ideas <kanji>stream</kanji> between them; that two-way movement is <vocabulary>exchange</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>interaction</vocabulary>.

交流 is reciprocal contact among people, groups, regions, or cultures, often with 交流する or 交流を深める.
words.readingMnemonic: Exchange 交 carries こう into a river, while flow 流 carries りゅう back upstream: <reading>こう—りゅう</reading>. Letters, people, and ideas ride both currents, creating constant <vocabulary>exchange</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>interaction</vocabulary> between two towns. 交流 often involves people, cultures, ideas, or electrical currents flowing both ways.

contextSentences.ja: 留学生との交流を楽しんだ。
contextSentences.en: I enjoyed interacting with international students.

contextSentences.ja: 地域の交流を深める行事です。
contextSentences.en: This event strengthens exchange within the community.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Your <kanji>body</kanji>'s <kanji>warm</kanji>th is its <vocabulary>body temperature</vocabulary>.

体温 is the measured temperature of a person or animal; 体温を測る means to take someone's temperature.
words.readingMnemonic: A nurse makes you <reading>TIE—ON</reading> a thermometer like a necktie. Its glowing number reveals your <vocabulary>body temperature</vocabulary>. 体温を測る means to measure someone's body temperature.

contextSentences.ja: 朝起きて体温を測った。
contextSentences.en: I measured my body temperature after waking up.

contextSentences.ja: 運動すると体温が上がる。
contextSentences.en: Exercise raises your body temperature.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Come <kanji>together</kanji> inside the same <kanji>feeling</kanji> and you experience <vocabulary>empathy</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>sympathy</vocabulary>.

共感 is an understood or shared emotional response, commonly expressed as Xに共感する.
words.readingMnemonic: Together 共 carries きょう as it ties two hearts together, then feeling 感 carries かん into both chests: <reading>きょう—かん</reading>. One friend's sadness now pulses inside the other as literal <vocabulary>empathy</vocabulary>. 共感 is sharing or relating to another person's feeling or viewpoint.

contextSentences.ja: 彼女の意見に強く共感した。
contextSentences.en: I strongly empathized with her opinion.

contextSentences.ja: この物語は多くの共感を集めた。
contextSentences.en: This story drew a great deal of sympathy.

words.meaningMnemonic:
One <kanji>friend</kanji> ties a ribbon carrying their deepest <kanji>feeling</kanji> to another friend's wrist; that bond is <vocabulary>friendship</vocabulary>.

友情 emphasizes the bond or affection between friends and often appears in expressions such as 友情を深める and 友情が続く.
words.readingMnemonic: You and Joe clasp hands over a canyon while everyone chants <reading>YOU—JOE</reading>. Trust keeps the bridge beneath you intact, turning your bond into visible <vocabulary>friendship</vocabulary>. 友情 refers to friendship as a bond or feeling.

contextSentences.ja: 二人の友情は長く続いた。
contextSentences.en: Their friendship lasted a long time.

contextSentences.ja: 試合の後で友情が深まった。
contextSentences.en: Their friendship deepened after the match.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Club members <kanji>join</kanji> one training plan and <kanji>lodge</kanji> under one roof, turning every waking hour into a <vocabulary>training camp</vocabulary>.

合宿 is an overnight group camp organized around a shared purpose, commonly sports, club practice, study, or work training.
words.readingMnemonic: At training camp, a leaking stove explodes and everyone yells <reading>GAS—SHOOK!</reading> The blast shakes the shared lodge, but the team stays to finish its <vocabulary>training camp</vocabulary>. 合宿 is a group stay for concentrated training or practice.

contextSentences.ja: 夏休みに部活の合宿がある。
contextSentences.en: Our club has a training camp during summer vacation.

contextSentences.ja: 合宿で毎日六時間練習した。
contextSentences.en: We practiced six hours every day at camp.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Let another source <kanji>participate</kanji> while you <kanji>think</kanji>; it becomes a <vocabulary>reference</vocabulary> for your decision.

参考 is information consulted for help rather than a command to follow; 参考にする means to use something as a reference.
words.readingMnemonic: Sun Co. keeps a library where every book glows like daylight: <reading>SUN—CO.</reading> A designer consults those volumes as a <vocabulary>reference</vocabulary> before making a decision. 参考にする means to use something for reference or guidance.

contextSentences.ja: この例を参考にしてください。
contextSentences.en: Please use this example as a reference.

contextSentences.ja: みんなの意見を参考にして決めた。
contextSentences.en: I decided after consulting everyone's opinions.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Tie each <kanji>flower</kanji> into one <kanji>bundle</kanji> and you have a <vocabulary>bouquet</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>bunch of flowers</vocabulary>.

花束 is a gathered arrangement intended to be carried or presented, especially as a gift or at a ceremony.
words.readingMnemonic: A flower 花 carries はな into a bundle 束 carrying たば: <reading>はな—たば</reading>. Every stem in the shop ties itself into one enormous <vocabulary>bouquet</vocabulary>. 花束 is a bound bunch of flowers, especially one given as a gift.

contextSentences.ja: 誕生日に花束をもらった。
contextSentences.en: I received a bouquet for my birthday.

contextSentences.ja: 駅で花束を持って彼女を待った。
contextSentences.en: I waited for her at the station holding a bunch of flowers.

words.meaningMnemonic:
After everyone <kanji>meet</kanji>s for a meal, <kanji>measure</kanji> what is owed: that total is the <vocabulary>bill</vocabulary>, and tracking such totals is <vocabulary>accounting</vocabulary>.

会計 means checkout or the bill in shops and restaurants, while in organizational settings it refers to accounts or accounting.
words.readingMnemonic: Kai and Kay stare at a restaurant receipt while the cashier calls <reading>KAI—KAY</reading>. They split the <vocabulary>bill</vocabulary>, then Kay runs the <vocabulary>checkout</vocabulary> twice to verify it. 会計 can mean payment at a shop or accounting more broadly.

contextSentences.ja: 会計を別々にできますか。
contextSentences.en: Can we pay the bill separately?

contextSentences.ja: 姉は会社で会計を担当している。
contextSentences.en: My sister handles accounting at her company.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Draw a line around each <kanji>district</kanji> to keep it <kanji>separate</kanji>; the boundary creates a <vocabulary>distinction</vocabulary> and lets you <vocabulary>differentiate</vocabulary> them.

区別 focuses on telling categories or things apart; 区別する is to distinguish, classify, or discriminate between them.
words.readingMnemonic: A pigeon cries COO over a mountain of betting slips: <reading>COO—BETS!</reading> It pecks red bets left and blue bets right, creating a strict <vocabulary>distinction</vocabulary> between them. 区別する means to distinguish or tell things apart.

contextSentences.ja: 赤と緑を区別しにくい。
contextSentences.en: It is hard to distinguish red from green.

contextSentences.ja: 大人用と子ども用を色で区別しています。
contextSentences.en: The adult and child versions are distinguished by color.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Give every <kanji>simple</kanji> step on a scale its own <kanji>rank</kanji>; each counted step is a <vocabulary>unit</vocabulary> or, at school, an <vocabulary>academic credit</vocabulary>.

単位 is a unit of measurement or a credit earned in a course; the surrounding noun tells you which system is being counted.
words.readingMnemonic: Professor Tan holds up a glowing letter E: <reading>TAN—E</reading>. That one E becomes both a measuring <vocabulary>unit</vocabulary> and the single <vocabulary>academic credit</vocabulary> every student needs. 単位 can mean a measurement unit or a university course credit.

contextSentences.ja: 長さの単位をメートルにそろえた。
contextSentences.en: We standardized the unit of length to meters.

contextSentences.ja: 卒業には百二十単位が必要です。
contextSentences.en: One hundred twenty credits are required to graduate.

words.meaningMnemonic:
A radio receiver must <kanji>accept</kanji> the signal, then light a green <kanji>trust</kanji> seal to confirm it arrived intact; this is how you <vocabulary>receive a message</vocabulary>, the process of <vocabulary>reception</vocabulary>.

受信 is used for receiving electronic signals, broadcasts, email, or data and contrasts with 送信, transmission.
words.readingMnemonic: Receive 受 carries じゅ into a radio, and trust 信 carries しん into its antenna: <reading>じゅ—しん</reading>. The radio flashes when it completes <vocabulary>reception</vocabulary> of a message or signal. 受信する is used for receiving broadcasts, data, email, or other signals.

contextSentences.ja: 先ほどメールを受信しました。
contextSentences.en: I received the email a moment ago.

contextSentences.ja: 山の中では電波を受信できない。
contextSentences.en: You cannot receive a signal in the mountains.

words.meaningMnemonic:
<kanji>Enter</kanji> the tub and <kanji>bathe</kanji>: that is <vocabulary>bathing</vocabulary>, or to <vocabulary>take a bath</vocabulary>.

入浴 is a somewhat formal noun or する verb for getting into a bath, common in instructions, schedules, health guidance, and facility notices.
words.readingMnemonic: Enter 入 carries にゅう as it dives through the door of a bath 浴 carrying よく: <reading>にゅう—よく</reading>. The bather splashes down fully clothed and has to <vocabulary>take a bath</vocabulary>. 入浴する is a formal-neutral way to describe bathing or taking a bath.

contextSentences.ja: 寝る前に入浴する。
contextSentences.en: I take a bath before bed.

contextSentences.ja: 食後すぐの入浴は避けてください。
contextSentences.en: Please avoid bathing immediately after eating.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Your <kanji>flavor</kanji> <kanji>awareness</kanji> is your <vocabulary>sense of taste</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>palate</vocabulary>.

味覚 is the sensory faculty itself, not an opinion about whether one particular food tastes good.
words.readingMnemonic: Taste 味 carries み onto the tongue, and awareness 覚 carries かく into a flashing flavor alarm: <reading>み—かく</reading>. The alarm identifies every ingredient through the tongue's <vocabulary>sense of taste</vocabulary>. 味覚 refers to the faculty of taste rather than one particular flavor.

contextSentences.ja: 風邪を引いて味覚が鈍くなった。
contextSentences.en: My sense of taste became dull after I caught a cold.

contextSentences.ja: 子どもの味覚は少しずつ変わる。
contextSentences.en: A child's palate changes little by little.

words.meaningMnemonic:
Picture an <kanji>individual</kanji> whose <kanji>gender</kanji> is only one tile in a much larger mosaic; the whole distinctive pattern is their <vocabulary>individuality</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>personality</vocabulary>.

個性 is the set of traits that makes a person, work, or place distinctive, often positively as character or uniqueness.
words.readingMnemonic: One individual 個 carries こ into a factory, while character 性 carries せい onto every worker's badge: <reading>こ—せい</reading>. No two badges match, so each person's <vocabulary>individuality</vocabulary> is impossible to miss. 個性 is the distinctive personality or character of a person or thing.

contextSentences.ja: この店には強い個性がある。
contextSentences.en: This shop has a strong personality.

contextSentences.ja: 子どもの個性を大切にしたい。
contextSentences.en: I want to value each child's individuality.

words.meaningMnemonic:
